record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether power-law scaling holds using acoustic APC models and development-set L1 loss rather than language models and held-out cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The reported loss is acoustic-model development-set L1 loss, not language-model cross-entropy. The paper does not report downstream-task results. Individual plotted measurements are not numerically stated in the text; rows capture reported fits and explicit conclusions, not figure-only point estimates.
record.test_reason: It fits power-law-plus-constant scaling laws to speech (APC acoustic model) pretraining loss against data, parameters and compute. This is a new modality with a direct result on V5, not a language-model reproduction, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that APC acoustic-model loss follows the joint power law of Eq. 3 in model size and data, with an irreducible loss term, over two orders of magnitude. They find a shared L∞ for LSTM and Transformer, suggesting it is a property of the data. They also report that training to convergence is inefficient, data needs scale sub-linearly with N, larger models learn faster, and Transformers scale more efficiently with compute than LSTMs.
record.recipe_differences: This is an acoustic-model extension rather than a language-model reproduction: it uses APC models, speech features, and development-set L1 loss rather than language-model cross-entropy. It also introduces a generalized fit with an irreducible-loss term.
record.method_sensitivity: The compute-frontier slope differs between the LSTM and Transformer systems.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger acoustic models reach lower development-set loss than smaller ones after processing the same data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models are more sample-efficient (learn faster per token or frame).

record.problems: The evidence is from one non-public 23 thousand hour English speech corpus and uses development-set L1 loss rather than cross-entropy. The paper gives no uncertainty estimates. It does not evaluate downstream task performance, and individual measurements shown in plots are not numerically reported in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Individual plotted points and separate model-size/data combinations in Figures 2–5 are not listed as rows because their numerical values are not stated in the text; the reported aggregate fits and explicit textual results are recorded instead.

untested.parts: Image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are untested. Only one non-public English far-field speech corpus with L1 loss is used, and no uncertainty is reported.
Parameter counting, schedule, data and fitting-method choices are not varied, and departures from a single power law are not tested.
Not tested; no language models are studied.
Not tested; there is no held-out extrapolation to larger runs.
Not tested; no compute-optimal N/D allocation is derived.
Not tested; aspect ratio is fixed after preliminary experiments with no reported numbers.
Not tested; downstream results are explicitly left to future work.

missing.what: Derived data/size trade-offs: a 5% loss reduction needs 14.0x data or 24.6x parameters; D > 0.0436 N^0.8230 is needed to avoid data limitation. Data-limited below about 1k hours, parameter-limited below about 2M parameters.
Fitted irreducible loss differs between the converged-model fits (0.316) and the compute-frontier fits (0.306); the authors attribute this to limited precision.

record.verdict_notes: The exponents are very small (about 0.014-0.02) and losses span a narrow range (about 0.316-0.345), so the fits are visual on log-log plots with no uncertainty reported. Individual points appear only in figures. Aspect ratios were chosen from unreported preliminary experiments, so there is no V4 evidence.

versions.untested_parts: The study is about acoustic models, not language models, and uses L1 loss rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy.
It does not report a procedure in which power laws fitted on small runs predict the losses of runs orders of magnitude larger.
The study does not identify the loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute or estimate how each grows with compute.
It does not compare depth and width at fixed parameter count across a wide range of architecture settings.
Tests acoustic APC models on one speech corpus using L1 loss; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The paper explicitly leaves relating its L1 loss to downstream acoustic-modeling performance for future work.

The study reports different compute-frontier slopes for LSTM and Transformer systems. It does not test alternative parameter-counting methods, fitting methods, or whether curves bend away from a power law.

relationships.condition: APC acoustic models (LSTM and Transformer) on a 23k-hour English speech corpus, development-set L1 loss
relationships.reason: Power-law-plus-constant fits in D, N, joint (N,D) and compute match the data over about two orders of magnitude (R1, R2, R3, R5, R6). R4 is derived from these fits.
relationships.display_finding: Power laws plus constants matched data, parameter, joint, and compute scaling over approximately two orders of magnitude.

relationships.condition: Compute-efficient frontier, LSTM versus Transformer acoustic models
relationships.reason: Frontier exponents differ by architecture (-0.167 vs -0.197), and fitted L∞ differs between analyses (0.316 vs 0.306) (R5, R6). This is only weak evidence of setup dependence.
relationships.display_finding: Frontier exponents are −0.167 for LSTMs and −0.197 for Transformers, while fitted asymptotic loss differs between analyses at 0.316 versus 0.306.
